prompt.context: The client is an industrial manufacturer of cranes. They are a French company and have recently acquired a US business to expand their product offering and also enter the US market. The two products are mobile cranes and tower cranes. The combined company holds approximately 60% of the global market. Currently the tower business, used for skyscrapers, is located in Europe. The mobile business, used for building highways, is located in the US. Prior to the acquisition, the company did have a small mobile manufacturer that they still retain.
prompt.question: The company has brought you and your team in to determine how to reduce redundancy and maintain a single face to the customer. The client also wants to explore the possibility of expanding mobile cranes into Europe and tower cranes into the US. Should they build new facilities or ship products?

clarifying_info.q: How does the company distribute its products?
clarifying_info.a: The distribution flow is: Manufacturer -> Dealer -> Construction firm (60% of revenue), and Manufacturer -> Construction firms directly (40% of revenue). The dealer often leases equipment to the end customer and is responsible for repairs. Their sales force must know the product.

clarifying_info.q: What is the current market share breakdown by product and region?
clarifying_info.a: Tower cranes: 80% share in Europe, 20% share in US. Mobile cranes: 40% share in Europe, 70% share in US. Total global market share is approximately 60%.

clarifying_info.q: Are dealers aware of the acquisition?
clarifying_info.a: Yes. The information about the merger/acquisition was communicated to dealers, so they had an expectation of being able to benefit from redundancy elimination. They will likely expect lower costs from the manufacturer because of redundancy elimination.

framework: Customer Confidence: Address the dealer relationship and manage expectations post-acquisition
Expansion Plans: Evaluate options for expanding mobile cranes into Europe and tower cranes into the US (build vs. ship)

questions.prompt: How should the company manage its dealer relationships post-acquisition?
questions.guidance: Managing the dealer relationship is key. Dealers will now face a larger cost of doing business because they must learn the sales pitch for the expanded product catalog and be prepared to service both mobile and tower cranes. This increases their cost base, so they will need higher margin to offset these costs. The client must balance redundancy elimination (which dealers expect to lower costs) against the reality that dealers face new burdens. A single, unified dealer interface is important for maintaining a single face to the customer.

questions.prompt: What are the options for expanding mobile cranes into Europe, and what are the pros and cons of each?
questions.guidance: There are three options for mobile crane expansion into Europe: (A) Expand the existing German facility — no action needed until it reaches 100% capacity; (B) Find/build new facilities in Europe — Pro: no tariffs; Con: capital investment required and need to find a suitable location; (C) Ship from the US to Europe — Pro: can serve as spillover for excess inventory; Con: tariffs apply, need sufficient scale to overcome competition and risk of competitor retaliation, and lead times are longer.

questions.prompt: What are the options for expanding tower cranes into the US, and what are the pros and cons of each?
questions.guidance: There are two options for tower crane expansion into the US: (A) Build new facilities in the US — Pro: no tariffs; Con: must first validate that US customer demand is sufficient to justify a new facility; (B) Ship from Europe — Pro: allows the company to manage competition if viewed as a small-scale entry; Con: tariffs apply, need sufficient scale to overcome competition, and lead times are longer.

questions.prompt: What was the actual solution in this real client engagement?
questions.guidance: In practice, the client maxed out production in Germany. In the US, they converted an existing facility to create a hybrid product between mobile and tower cranes that could handle small- to mid-sized projects. This avoided the capital investment required by an entirely new facility while still enabling market entry. The company gained significant market share as a result.

brainstorming.prompt: What factors should the company consider when deciding between building a new facility versus shipping products across regions?

categories.name: Cost Factors
ideas: Tariffs and import duties on cross-border shipments
Capital expenditure required for a new facility
Ongoing operating costs of a new facility vs. incremental shipping costs
Existing facility utilization and expansion capacity

categories.name: Market and Demand
ideas: Level of customer demand in the target region to justify fixed investment
Competitive response if entry is seen as significant vs. insignificant
Ability to gain sufficient market share to achieve economies of scale
Lead time sensitivity of customers in the target region

categories.name: Operational Considerations
ideas: Proximity to customers and dealers for service support
Logistics complexity of long-distance shipping of large equipment
Ability to leverage existing manufacturing know-how in a new location
Hybrid product opportunities that leverage existing assets

categories.name: Strategic Fit
ideas: Alignment with the goal of maintaining a single face to the customer
Impact on dealer network and dealer economics
Synergies from combining tower and mobile crane expertise

recommendation: Prioritize eliminating redundancy by unifying the dealer network and product catalog, while proactively managing dealer expectations about margin impact
For mobile cranes in Europe, first maximize the German facility before committing to new capital investment; use shipping as a bridge for excess inventory
For tower cranes in the US, validate demand before building; consider converting or adapting an existing US facility to create a hybrid product that avoids full greenfield capital outlay
risks: Dealer dissatisfaction if margin expectations are not met after acquisition synergies are communicated
Tariff exposure if shipping is used as a long-term strategy
Competitor retaliation if entry into new markets is perceived as a significant threat
Insufficient demand in new markets to justify fixed investment in new facilities
next_steps: Conduct a detailed assessment of German facility capacity and timeline to 100% utilization
Survey US customer demand for tower cranes to validate market entry economics
Model build-vs-ship financials including tariffs, capex, and breakeven volume for each option
Develop a dealer communication and margin-sharing plan to retain dealer loyalty post-acquisition
